These contracts provide that the purchase price will be paid by the buyer and accepted by the seller in installments over an agreed-upon period. The vendor keeps legal title to the property as security for the buyer's payment obligations, and the vendee obtains equitable title through the doctrine of equitable conversion. Perhaps the most critical element of the installment land contract is the forfeiture provision, under which a vendee who remains in default for 30 days faces the possibility that the vendor may elect to declare a forfeiture. Upon such a declaration, all payments already made are forfeited as "liquidated" damages, and the buyer is relegated to tenant-at-will status. Throughout the years, property sellers have frequently declared forfeitures against delinquent buyers under these arrangements, sometimes even when the buyer had missed only one payment after having satisfied nearly all other installments. In response to this inequitable outcome, the state legislature adopted a new statute that compels any seller who wishes to declare a forfeiture of an installment land contract to do so through a formal judicial foreclosure proceeding. Furthermore, the law requires that the seller afford the buyer a 60-day grace period to pay any delinquent installment with interest before any foreclosure action can be commenced. By its express terms, the statute applies to installment land contracts entered into after its enactment as well as to those already in existence when it was enacted. Over the years, many sellers of property under such installment land contracts have declared forfeitures in situations where the prospective buyers were delinquent in their payments, even when the buyer was late with a single payment after nearly all the other payments had been made. In order to remedy this inequitable situation, the state legislature enacted a statute requiring any seller attempting to declare a forfeiture of an installment land contract to do so by instituting a formal foreclosure action in the courts. The new law also provided that prior to the commencement of such a foreclosure action, the seller under such an arrangement must give the buyer a 60-day grace period to make up any delinquent installment payment with interest. The seller maintains legal title as collateral for the purchase price, while the buyer holds equitable title pursuant to the doctrine of equitable conversion. The most significant feature of the installment land contract is its forfeiture clause, which stipulates that if the buyer defaults for 30 days, the seller may, at his discretion, declare the contract forfeited. In that event, all payments previously made are treated as "liquidated" damages, and the buyer becomes a tenant at will of the seller. To address this unjust situation, the state legislature passed a law mandating that any seller seeking to declare a forfeiture of an installment land contract must initiate a formal foreclosure proceeding in court. Additionally, the statute required that before commencing any such foreclosure action, the seller must provide the buyer with a 60-day grace period to cure any overdue installment payment along with interest. It is known that for many years, parties to real estate transactions in a certain state have made frequent use of installment land contracts as a popular substitute for mortgages or deeds of trust. In these contracts, the buyer agrees to pay and the seller agrees to accept the purchase price through installments spread over a specified period. Legal title is retained by the vendor as security for payment, while the vendee acquires equitable title under the equitable conversion doctrine. The defining characteristic of such contracts, however, is the forfeiture clause: should the vendee be in default for 30 days, the vendor has the option to declare the contract forfeited, whereupon all prior payments are retained as "liquidated" damages and the buyer is reduced to the status of a tenant at will. Historically, many sellers have exercised this forfeiture right when buyers became delinquent on payments — even in instances where a buyer was late on just one payment after having completed nearly all other installments. Seeking to correct this inequitable practice, the state legislature enacted legislation that requires sellers wishing to declare a forfeiture under an installment land contract to pursue a formal foreclosure action through the courts. Under this new law, the seller must also grant the buyer a 60-day grace period before initiating foreclosure, during which the buyer may pay any overdue installment plus interest. The legislation was made explicitly applicable to installment land contracts formed after its enactment as well as to those that were already in effect when it was enacted. Is this newly enacted state statute likely to withstand constitutional scrutiny?

According to established practice, real estate participants in a state have long employed installment land contracts as a common alternative to mortgages and deeds of trust. These contracts provide that the purchase price will be paid by the buyer and accepted by the seller in installments over an agreed-upon period. The vendor keeps legal title to the property as security for the buyer's payment obligations, and the vendee obtains equitable title through the doctrine of equitable conversion. Perhaps the most critical element of the installment land contract is the forfeiture provision, under which a vendee who remains in default for 30 days faces the possibility that the vendor may elect to declare a forfeiture. Upon such a declaration, all payments already made are forfeited as "liquidated" damages, and the buyer is relegated to tenant-at-will status. Throughout the years, property sellers have frequently declared forfeitures against delinquent buyers under these arrangements, sometimes even when the buyer had missed only one payment after having satisfied nearly all other installments. In response to this inequitable outcome, the state legislature adopted a new statute that compels any seller who wishes to declare a forfeiture of an installment land contract to do so through a formal judicial foreclosure proceeding. Furthermore, the law requires that the seller afford the buyer a 60-day grace period to pay any delinquent installment with interest before any foreclosure action can be commenced. By its express terms, the statute applies to installment land contracts entered into after its enactment as well as to those already in existence when it was enacted. Is this new state statute likely to be upheld as constitutional?

I am of opinion that the principal and true profession of the Courtier ought to be that of arms; which I would have him follow actively above all else, and be known among others as bold and strong, and loyal to whomsoever he serves. . . .
I would have him well built and shapely of limb, and would have him show strength and lightness and suppleness, and know all bodily exercises that befit a man of war; whereof I think the first should be to handle every sort of weapon well on foot and on horse, to understand the advantages of each, and especially to be familiar with those weapons that are ordinarily used among gentlemen. . . .
Our Courtier then will be esteemed excellent and will attain grace in everything, particularly in speaking. . . .
I would have him more than passably accomplished in letters, at least in those studies that are called the humanities, and conversant not only with the Latin language but with the Greek, for the sake of the many different things that have been admirably written therein. Let him be well versed in the poets, and not less in the orators and historians, and also proficient in writing verse and prose, especially in this vulgar [vernacular] tongue of ours. . . .
You must know that I am not content with the Courtier unless he be also a musician and unless, besides understanding and being able to read notes, he can play upon divers instruments. . . .
I wish our Courtier to guard against getting the name of a liar or a boaster, which sometimes befalls even those who do not deserve it.
—From Baldassare Castiglione's Book of the Courtier, 1528

source_question: For many years, persons engaged in real estate transactions in a state have utilized installment land contracts. The so-called installment land contract has been popular as a substitute for the mortgage or deed of trust. Under such a contract, the seller agrees to accept, and the buyer agrees to pay, the purchase price in installments over a stipulated period of time. The vendor retains legal title as security for the payment of the purchase price; and the vendee has equitable title under the doctrine of equitable conversion. The most important characteristic of the installment land contract, however, is the forfeiture clause, which provides that if the vendee is in default for 30 days, the vendor may, at his option, declare a forfeiture of the contract, in which case all payments made shall be forfeited as "liquidated" damages and the buyer shall become a tenant at will of the seller. Over the years, many sellers of property under such installment land contracts have declared forfeitures in situations where the prospective buyers were delinquent in their payments, even when the buyer was late with a single payment after nearly all the other payments had been made. In order to remedy this inequitable situation, the state legislature enacted a statute requiring any seller attempting to declare a forfeiture of an installment land contract to do so by instituting a formal foreclosure action in the courts. The new law also provided that prior to the commencement of such a foreclosure action, the seller under such an arrangement must give the buyer a 60-day grace period to make up any delinquent installment payment with interest. The new law expressly applied both to installment land contracts entered into subsequent to its enactment and to installment land contracts already in existence at the time of its enactment. Is this new state statute likely to be held constitutional?
variants: For many years, individuals involved in real estate dealings within a particular state have relied on installment land contracts. These contracts have served as a widely used alternative to mortgages or deeds of trust. Under such an agreement, the seller consents to receive, and the buyer consents to pay, the purchase price in periodic installments over a defined timeframe. The seller maintains legal title as collateral for the purchase price, while the buyer holds equitable title pursuant to the doctrine of equitable conversion. The most significant feature of the installment land contract is its forfeiture clause, which stipulates that if the buyer defaults for 30 days, the seller may, at his discretion, declare the contract forfeited. In that event, all payments previously made are treated as "liquidated" damages, and the buyer becomes a tenant at will of the seller. Over time, numerous property sellers operating under these contracts have invoked forfeiture provisions against buyers who fell behind on payments, including cases where the buyer missed only a single payment after having made nearly all prior installments. To address this unjust situation, the state legislature passed a law mandating that any seller seeking to declare a forfeiture of an installment land contract must initiate a formal foreclosure proceeding in court. Additionally, the statute required that before commencing any such foreclosure action, the seller must provide the buyer with a 60-day grace period to cure any overdue installment payment along with interest. The statute was made expressly applicable to both installment land contracts created after its passage and those already existing at the time it took effect. Is this new state law likely to be deemed constitutional?

It is known that for many years, parties to real estate transactions in a certain state have made frequent use of installment land contracts as a popular substitute for mortgages or deeds of trust. In these contracts, the buyer agrees to pay and the seller agrees to accept the purchase price through installments spread over a specified period. Legal title is retained by the vendor as security for payment, while the vendee acquires equitable title under the equitable conversion doctrine. The defining characteristic of such contracts, however, is the forfeiture clause: should the vendee be in default for 30 days, the vendor has the option to declare the contract forfeited, whereupon all prior payments are retained as "liquidated" damages and the buyer is reduced to the status of a tenant at will. Historically, many sellers have exercised this forfeiture right when buyers became delinquent on payments — even in instances where a buyer was late on just one payment after having completed nearly all other installments. Seeking to correct this inequitable practice, the state legislature enacted legislation that requires sellers wishing to declare a forfeiture under an installment land contract to pursue a formal foreclosure action through the courts. Under this new law, the seller must also grant the buyer a 60-day grace period before initiating foreclosure, during which the buyer may pay any overdue installment plus interest. The legislation was made explicitly applicable to installment land contracts formed after its enactment as well as to those that were already in effect when it was enacted. Is this newly enacted state statute likely to withstand constitutional scrutiny?

According to established practice, real estate participants in a state have long employed installment land contracts as a common alternative to mortgages and deeds of trust. These contracts provide that the purchase price will be paid by the buyer and accepted by the seller in installments over an agreed-upon period. The vendor keeps legal title to the property as security for the buyer's payment obligations, and the vendee obtains equitable title through the doctrine of equitable conversion. Perhaps the most critical element of the installment land contract is the forfeiture provision, under which a vendee who remains in default for 30 days faces the possibility that the vendor may elect to declare a forfeiture. Upon such a declaration, all payments already made are forfeited as "liquidated" damages, and the buyer is relegated to tenant-at-will status. Throughout the years, property sellers have frequently declared forfeitures against delinquent buyers under these arrangements, sometimes even when the buyer had missed only one payment after having satisfied nearly all other installments. In response to this inequitable outcome, the state legislature adopted a new statute that compels any seller who wishes to declare a forfeiture of an installment land contract to do so through a formal judicial foreclosure proceeding. Furthermore, the law requires that the seller afford the buyer a 60-day grace period to pay any delinquent installment with interest before any foreclosure action can be commenced. By its express terms, the statute applies to installment land contracts entered into after its enactment as well as to those already in existence when it was enacted. Is this new state statute likely to be upheld as constitutional?

Legal title is retained by the vendor as security for payment, while the vendee acquires equitable title under the equitable conversion doctrine. The defining characteristic of such contracts, however, is the forfeiture clause: should the vendee be in default for 30 days, the vendor has the option to declare the contract forfeited, whereupon all prior payments are retained as "liquidated" damages and the buyer is reduced to the status of a tenant at will. Historically, many sellers have exercised this forfeiture right when buyers became delinquent on payments — even in instances where a buyer was late on just one payment after having completed nearly all other installments. Seeking to correct this inequitable practice, the state legislature enacted legislation that requires sellers wishing to declare a forfeiture under an installment land contract to pursue a formal foreclosure action through the courts. Under this new law, the seller must also grant the buyer a 60-day grace period before initiating foreclosure, during which the buyer may pay any overdue installment plus interest. The legislation was made explicitly applicable to installment land contracts formed after its enactment as well as to those that were already in effect when it was enacted.
